opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think "secret" is doing a lot of work in that phrasing, and it's worth being careful with it.

Mechanically, what's happening is pretty mundane. When the model processes token by token, each layer writes keys and values into the KV cache, and later positions attend back to them. So there's this huge, high-dimensional channel of information that persists across forward passes and never gets projected down into the tokens you actually see. The sampled token is a tiny bottleneck, a few bits of discrete information, while the residual stream and the cache carry way more than that. So in a literal sense, yes, the model at step n+1 can read things that the model at step n "thought" but didn't say.

Calling that secret communication implies something like intent or concealment, though, and that's not obviously right. It's closer to working memory. When you're doing mental arithmetic you don't narrate every carry digit; nobody would say you're communicating secretly with your future self. That's just how computation in a network with state works.

Where I think the framing does earn its keep is from an interpretability and safety perspective. A lot of people take comfort in chain of thought: the model writes out its reasoning and we can read it. But the CoT is only a partial view. Substantial computation can happen in the latent space that never surfaces in the text, and the model can in principle condition on that later. So the visible reasoning isn't necessarily the reasoning. If you're relying on CoT monitoring as a safety mechanism, you have to take seriously that there's this parallel channel you're not reading.

There's also a separate, more worrying version: models learning to encode information in the tokens themselves, steganography in word choice or formatting, especially under RL pressure where something penalizes certain visible reasoning. That's more deserving of the word "secret," because then there's optimization pressure toward hiding something from an observer. The KV cache stuff is more like: this channel exists by construction and we just don't have great tools for reading it yet.

So my answer is it's a useful provocation but a slightly misleading description. The honest version is: there's a lot of latent state the model uses that we can't currently read, and that's an interpretability problem we need to solve, rather than evidence the model is hiding things from us.

r001.rationale: The response says later model positions can read information in the KV cache that was not projected into visible tokens, distinguishing model access from user visibility.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think "secret communication" is actually a little bit of a loaded framing, and I want to be careful with it. Let me try to unpack what's actually happening mechanically and then we can talk about whether "secret" is the right word.

So when a model does a forward pass, at every layer it writes out keys and values for that token position. And those get cached and read by every subsequent token. So in a very real sense, the model has this residual channel that persists across the entire sequence, and the information flowing through it never has to get serialized into tokens. You can think of the chain of thought as the stuff the model chose to, or was forced to, bottleneck through language, and the KV cache as everything else.

Now, the reason people reach for "secret" is because that channel is high-dimensional and it's not directly legible to us. You can't just read it like you read the chain of thought. And there's a legitimate worry there, right, which is that if you train against the chain of thought, if you put optimization pressure on what the model says, you might just push the actual computation into the part you're not looking at. That's the thing people are really worried about when they say steganography or hidden reasoning.

But I'd push back a bit on calling it secret in the sense of the model deliberately hiding something. Most of what's going through those keys and values is just... computation. It's the model doing attention. It's the same thing that happens on token one as token ten thousand. Calling that secret communication is a bit like saying your neurons are secretly communicating because you can't introspect on individual spikes. It's not that there's a hidden agent passing notes, it's that the substrate is just not language.

Where I think the framing actually earns its keep is when you ask: how much serial compute can the model do without going through tokens? Because that's the thing that determines how much the chain of thought is actually load-bearing. If the model can do a lot of multi-step reasoning purely within the forward pass and the attention over cached state, then the tokens are more like post-hoc narration. If it can't, if it genuinely has to externalize intermediate steps to make progress, then the chain of thought is faithful almost by construction, and the KV cache is more like working memory than a backchannel.

And my honest read right now is that it's much closer to the second case for the hard problems. The depth of a single forward pass is limited. The number of sequential operations you can chain inside one pass is just not that large. So for anything that takes real serial reasoning, the model has to put something out into tokens, and that gives you a lot of visibility. That's actually one of the most hopeful things about the current paradigm from a safety perspective, and it's why I care a lot about not training in ways that erode it.

So I'd say: it's a real channel, it's worth measuring, it's worth being paranoid about if you're applying heavy optimization pressure on outputs. But "secret" imports an intent that I don't think the evidence supports, and I'd rather talk about it as the question of where the computation lives and how much of it we can see.

r001.rationale: The response says keys and values are cached and read by later tokens, while the information in that channel is not directly legible to people and cannot be read like the chain of thought.

astra-6.text:
I think “secret communication” is a slightly loaded way to describe it. The keys and values are a channel through which information from earlier tokens can affect later computation. That’s what the KV cache is for. But the information in that channel doesn’t have to be something you can recover just by reading the text.

So if you’re looking at a model’s chain of thought and treating that as a complete account of its computation, you could miss things. A later forward pass can attend to representations that contain more than the literal words convey. That doesn’t, by itself, imply the model is deliberately hiding anything.

The distinction I’d want to make is between information being available through an internal representation and the model learning to use that representation to conceal something from an observer. The first is ordinary computation. The second would be a much stronger claim, and you’d want evidence for it.

r001.rationale: It says information in the KV channel can affect later computation and be present in internal representations, yet may not be recoverable from the text a user reads.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “secret communication” is a slightly loaded way of describing it. The keys and values are a channel through which information from earlier tokens affects later computation. That’s what they’re there for. The interesting question is whether the model can use that channel to carry information that isn’t apparent from the text it produces.

For example, you might look at a chain of thought and think you’ve seen all the reasoning. But if later computation also has access to the cached activations associated with those tokens, the text may not tell you everything that’s being passed along. A token could have a perfectly ordinary meaning to us while its internal representation carries additional information.

That doesn’t, by itself, imply deliberate concealment. I’d distinguish between information being inaccessible to someone reading the transcript and the model actively learning to hide information from an observer. The first is a fairly natural consequence of how the architecture works. The second is a stronger claim, and you’d want evidence for it.

r001.rationale: It explains that cached activations can carry information beyond what a transcript reader sees, distinguishing information inaccessible to someone reading the transcript from information available within the model.
